summary:
NightTrace is an independent web application that helps anyone explore how the sky changes using real NASA SPHEREx observations.

Users can select a region on an interactive sky map or open prepared examples featuring Pluto, the Cat's Eye Nebula, and Orion. They can compare dates using a sliding divider, blinking images, individual frames, and a difference view when the required checks pass.

Our key idea is simple: seeing a difference is only the beginning. Different wavelengths, image alignment, and pixel quality can create misleading changes. NightTrace displays comparison checks and explains limitations, helping users investigate before drawing conclusions.

Our Pluto example shows a known object moving across six observations from April 25-27, 2026, with positions compared against JPL DE421 predictions. A contrasting nebula example shows why images with different spectral coverage cannot establish a brightness change over time.

Users can mark possible changes in sky coordinates, add notes, and save reproducible observations through shareable links, JSON files, or printable cards.

Built with Python Flask and a lightweight web interface, NightTrace uses public NASA/IPAC IRSA data and requires no API keys. It supports English and Russian, light and dark themes, and responsive layouts. The final version passed 56 automated tests.

NightTrace turns curiosity into an investigation others can revisit. Every change leaves a trace.
details:
NightTrace helps anyone explore changes in the sky using real NASA SPHEREx observations. Users select a sky region or open examples such as Pluto, compare dates through blinking images, a sliding divider, or a difference view, and mark possible changes.

Built with Python, Flask, NumPy, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, the application retrieves public NASA/IPAC IRSA data, reads selected portions of FITS files, and aligns images on a shared coordinate grid. We used GitHub for version control and included Vercel deployment configuration. The final version passed 56 automated tests.

Our creative approach combines discovery with verification. A visible difference may result from motion, different wavelengths, or image artifacts. NightTrace checks spectral overlap, alignment, coverage, and quality, explains uncertainty, and restricts difference mode when required conditions fail. Pluto demonstrates known motion; a nebula example illustrates a potentially misleading brightness difference.

Users can save marks in sky coordinates, add notes, and share reproducible observations through links, JSON files, or printable cards.

We considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, archive reliability, and reproducibility. English and Russian interfaces, themes, keyboard controls, and responsive layouts broaden access. Our intended impact is to make astronomical exploration approachable while teaching users to question, document, and verify what they see.
